---
title: "NLP Evidence"
---

## Corpus and purpose

Our corpus contains ten nonempty descriptions. The saved text-cleaning summary reports a median of 917 words, a minimum of 228, and a maximum of 1,510. We decode HTML entities, remove markup and URLs, normalize case and whitespace, and preserve technical symbols. The NLP dictionary provides a narrower text check alongside the prepared skill bridge.

## Three distinct evidence measures

Source labels are the skills explicitly supplied in the original fields. Narrow text matches use the fixed 22-skill NLP dictionary. Combined evidence is the prepared bridge used by the final model and skill-gap analysis; it includes normalized source labels and broader preparation keyword rules. Counts are distinct postings, and the three columns should not be added together.

{{< include _generated/skill_source_comparison.qmd >}}

MLOps appears in five combined-evidence postings, while three carry source labels and three match the narrower dictionary. Two C3 Iot descriptions contain joined wording such as `DataOpsandMLOpsin`. The broader preparation rule detects MLOps there; the narrow word-boundary rule misses it. The source distinction explains the count difference and is carried into our [skill-gap interpretation](skill_gap_analysis.qmd).

The final build reproduces every saved narrow NLP posting–skill pair. That is a reproducibility check, not a precision or recall estimate against human annotations. A match does not establish whether a skill is required, preferred, or needed at a particular proficiency level.

## Supporting term exploration

The earlier TF-IDF workflow used one-word and two-word terms, minimum document frequency two, maximum document frequency 90%, and English plus domain stop words. Leading saved terms include `ai`, `business`, `ll`, `models`, and `time`. The contraction fragment `ll` and generic terms show why term weights require review. We do not treat TF-IDF rankings as skill-demand estimates.

Our [final segmentation](final_analytics.qmd) uses 37 recurring skills from combined evidence. A next improvement is a human-labeled extraction evaluation covering synonyms, negation, and required-versus-preferred language.
